title: microburst-lattice-scan
content:
Purpose:
Quick, messy lab notebook for a microburst-lattice run that surfaced an interesting interaction between kernel-switch overhead and thermal/GPU clock stepping when mixing tiny and large requests across two model families (Llama-variant + opt-style).

Hypothesis:
- Short requests (10-80 tokens) interleaved with long (600-1024 tokens) create a 'lattice' of small KV cache warmups + frequent kernel context switching.
- When bursts cross a thermal threshold, GPU clocks throttle and per-token latency for all requests jumps non-linearly due to longer kernel setup times.

Setup:
- Hardware: 1x A100-40GB, driver 525.xx, CUDA 12.1
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, nvidia-utils 525.60
- Runtime commit: serving-runtime@6fe2b4d (linked PR above)
- Models: llama-13b-quant (4-bit), opt-6.7b-fp16 (baseline)
- Batch config: dynamic batching on, max_batch_tokens=8192, batch_timeout_ms=6
- KV cache: enabled, per-request caching TTL=45s
- Traffic generator: custom harness (python) - reproduces lattice pattern: short,short,long,short,long,long,... with controllable inter-arrival drift

Pattern params used (representative run):
- Short reqs tokens: 20 +/- 8, 40% of traffic
- Long reqs tokens: 800 +/- 120, 60% of traffic
- Average QPS injected: 32 (bursty windows to 180 qps for 4s every 30s)
- Duration: 30m run with 6 warmup minutes

Metrics captured:
- p50/p95/p99 cold/warm split, GPU util %, GPU clock, power draw, kernel-latency trace (approx via perf counters), KV cache hit rate, batch sizes seen, queue length distribution

Key numbers (from 2024-11-06 13:22 run):
- Overall throughput sustained (avg): 29 QPS
- p50 latency (warm): 48 ms (short), 620 ms (long)
- p95 latency (warm): 140 ms (short), 1,020 ms (long)
- p99 latency (warm): 420 ms (short), 1,800 ms (long)
- During burst windows (180 qps spikes): p99 short jumped to 1.2s, long to 3.6s
- GPU util: 85% steady, but dips to 55% right after thermal step events
- KV cache hit rate: 62% for short requests (warm window), 18% for long (expected)
- Observed batch sizes: mean 3.2 reqs/batch, but reduced to ~1.2 at peak saturation (high arrival variance)

Notable observations:
- Thermal events: at ~18 minutes we saw power draw increase then GPU clock drop ~200 MHz; immediately following, kernel-setup times (observed via driver trace) increased by 2x for ~60s. This correlated with a burst of long requests.
- Kernel-switch overhead: when batches contained mixed short+long, the effective per-token time for short requests was >1.8x compared to short-only batches. Suspect expensive memcpy/path for switching FP16 vs quant kernels.
- Batching fallback: dynamic batching at 6ms timeout caused many short requests to be coalesced with a pending long, hurting short latency. Increasing batch_timeout to 2ms improved short p95 by ~30% but decreased long throughput slightly.
- Cache priming: injecting a tiny synthetic prefix to warm KV for long requests reduced long p95 by ~12% on average (but added cost).

Quick ascii sketch (latency timeline snippet):
TS     | short p95 | long p95 | GPU clock
13:21  | 160ms     | 980ms    | 1110 MHz
13:22  | 430ms     | 1820ms   | 910 MHz (post-throttle)
13:23  | 200ms     | 1050ms   | 1110 MHz (recovered)

Initial takeaways / actionables:
- Add a scheduling heuristic: avoid coalescing tiny requests with any request > X tokens in the same batch. (X ~ 256 tokens seems promising).
- Investigate kernel hot-path: add tracing around memcpy / kernel-selection when switching between quantized and fp16 kernels. Opened GH PR to add micro-prof counters in runtime.
- Try adaptive batch_timeout that is occupancy-aware: shorten timeout when queue has a mix of tiny requests.
- Add thermal-aware routing: if recent power/clock flaps detected, prefer routing long jobs to quieter nodes or reduced concurrency.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- replicate with 2x A100 (multi-GPU) and with mixed GPU types (V100-like) to see if kernel-switch overhead persists.
- run controlled experiment with pure short-only, pure long-only, and 50/50 interleave to measure isolation loss.
- capture driver-level perf counters next run (smaller interval) and save raw traces (they're big).
- sync with Keisha about trying modified batching heuristic (she has a draft scheduler change).

Links / references:
- GH PR with micro counters: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842
- Linear: LIN-1783 (microburst lattice followup)
- Slack thread: #eng-runtime threads p14567 (attached sensor logs)

Final note: this one felt like a crossover bug between scheduling policy and low-level kernel selection. If scheduler prevents mixed batches, most of the short-tail pain disappears. But that may increase cost (less packing). Need cost/latency tradeoff experiment next.

-- tchen
